sits just beyond visible light on the electromagnetic spectrum, invisible to the human eye, and every roof gives it off. The sun loads the membrane with radiant heat by day; after sunset, radiational cooling sets in as the roof radiates that heat to a clear sky. Wet insulation carries higher mass and retains heat longer than dry areas of lower mass, and that uneven heat dissipation leaves heat signatures a thermal imaging camera records. Temperature patterns in the thermal images indicate potential moisture issues: a thermogram of the heat signatures shows the wet areas as warm patches, and the recorded difference between wet and dry areas is what lets the survey identify saturated insulation.

faqs.q: What standard governs a roof thermal imaging inspection in Orange?

runs.v: ASTM C1153, the Standard Practice for Location of Wet Insulation in Roofing Systems Using Infrared Imaging, governs a roof thermal imaging inspection and ranks as the most commonly used infrared roof moisture standard, per ASTM and the NRCA. It applies the same way to a Valley Arts loft roof and a Main Street commercial roof, and it requires verification of every suspected wet area by core cut, probe, or calibrated moisture meter.

faqs.q: Why does infrared thermal imaging suit Orange's rental and Valley Arts loft roofs?

runs.v: It reads the roof from above without entering the occupied units below, where interior access follows New Jersey landlord-tenant notice, per IIBEC, and once the membrane cools after sunset the saturated insulation, which releases heat more slowly, glows as a warm anomaly within reach of modern infrared thermal imaging, per Fluke and IIBEC.

faqs.q: Can an infrared roof scan be done during the day in Orange?

runs.v: No. The scan runs after sunset, because ASTM C1153 sets optimal conditions of a clear sunny day followed by a clear night, when the dry membrane releases its heat fast and the wet area holds a sharp warm contrast, per ASTM C1153 via IIBEC and Fluke.

faqs.q: Does a thermal imaging inspection in Orange require a permit, and what about historic districts?

runs.v: No. The scan documents condition and triggers no permit; the repair it leads to follows N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, where a reroof on a detached one- or two-family home is ordinary maintenance and a commercial or multi-family job past 25% of the roof in 12 months needs a construction permit. A property inside a historic district can need extra review for the roofing work, so confirm current requirements with the City of Orange Township construction office before work begins.

faqs.q: Does thermal imaging find the exact leak entry point on an Orange building?

runs.v: No. Thermal imaging locates wet insulation rather than the leak entry point, because the wet footprint sits displaced from the breach and an infrared camera detects temperature patterns rather than water directly, per Fluke, IIBEC, and the NRCA. An infrared camera can still detect the wet area a roof leak or water leak leaves behind, and a core cut, probe, or calibrated moisture meter confirms each anomaly under ASTM C1153.
